meta.title: Analyzing Graphs — Water Usage During a Typical School Day
meta.pageTitle: Analyzing Graphs: Water Usage During a School Day | Hesten's Learning
meta.description: How does a physical building communicate through data? Examine cumulative volume graphs, interpret piecewise slopes, and calculate average rates of change across the rhythm of a high school day.
meta.pageDescription: Analyze piecewise rate of change, slope, and domain intervals on real-world continuous graphs of water consumption.
meta.author: Hesten's Learning Team

overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 4
overview.text: In this lesson, you will analyze a continuous graph representing cumulative water consumption over time. By observing how the slope steepens, flattens, or remains constant, you will connect graphical features directly to real-world physical events.
outcomes: Interpret key features of a graph (intercepts, intervals of increase, flat horizontal segments) in terms of the quantities modeled.
Calculate the average rate of change $\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta t} = \frac{V(t_2) - V(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}$ over specified time intervals.
Explain why a cumulative volume graph can never have a negative slope in a closed system without return flow.
overview.teacherInsight: A common misconception is that a flat horizontal line means "water is turned off and empty." Emphasize that on a cumulative graph, a flat line means volume is constant ($V(t)$ is unchanged, flow rate is zero), not that the tank is depleted!

content.html:
School Day Water Consumption Simulator

Drag the time scrubber from 6:00 AM to 8:00 PM. Watch how the cumulative volume curve ascends and inspect how instantaneous flow rates correlate with school activities.

Key Periods:
Time of Day (t): 12:00 PM
6 AM 8 AM 10 AM 12 PM 2 PM 4 PM 6 PM 8 PM
Cumulative Total $V(t)$ 1,950 gal Measured meter total since 6:00 AM
Flow Rate (Slope) 420 gal/hr Instantaneous rate of change
Lunch Period: Peak cafeteria dishwashing & restroom traffic.
Slope represents flow rate: Flatter = minimal use • Steeper = heavy flow

vocabulary.definition: The total aggregated quantity of water used up to a specified point in time.
The ratio of change in water volume to elapsed time: \Delta V / \Delta t.
A segment where slope m = 0, indicating zero flow rate or usage.

practiceQuestions.question: Suppose researchers collect school water consumption data through the night. For the period between when the last person leaves in the evening and the arrival of the first person the next morning, how should the graph of total cumulative water consumption appear?
options: As a flat horizontal line ($m = 0$), because no additional water is being consumed while the school is unoccupied.
As a steeply declining line dropping to zero, because the school is empty.
As a vertical line segment representing instantaneous drainage.
As an exponential curve increasing toward infinity.
practiceQuestions.explanation: From the official Eureka Math Exit Ticket Key: Cumulative water consumption remains constant when no water is drawn, resulting in a horizontal line with slope $m = 0$.

practiceQuestions.question: During those same unoccupied night hours, how should a graph of the rate of water consumption (in gallons per hour) appear?
options: A horizontal line resting directly on the horizontal axis at $y = 0\text{ gal/hr}$.
A curved parabola peaking at midnight.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Because no water is being consumed, the instantaneous rate of consumption is zero, so the rate curve sits flat at $y = 0$.

guidedExercises.title: Example 1: Piecewise Hourly Water Usage Rate Analysis
guidedExercises.problem: The cumulative water usage $W(t)$ of a school (in gallons) from 6:00 AM ($t = 0$) to 4:00 PM ($t = 10$) is recorded. From 7:00 AM to 8:00 AM (arrival), $W(t)$ rises from $100$ to $900$ gallons. From 8:00 AM to 11:00 AM (classes), $W(t)$ rises from $900$ to $1,500$ gallons. Calculate the average hourly consumption rate for both periods and interpret a horizontal segment on a cumulative graph.
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Calculate rate using $\frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}$. A horizontal segment on a cumulative graph means no change in volume occurred.

steps.label: Arrival Period: $t \in [1, 2]$ (7:00 AM - 8:00 AM)
steps.explanation: Intense usage as students and staff arrive, use restrooms, and prepare cafeteria meals.

steps.label: Class Period: $t \in [2, 5]$ (8:00 AM - 11:00 AM)
steps.explanation: Low, steady baseline usage while students are seated in classrooms.

steps.label: Interpret horizontal line segments
steps.explanation: On a cumulative graph, zero slope means zero water is consumed over that time interval.

guidedExercises.finalAnswer: \text{Arrival Rate: } 800\text{ gal/hr}; \quad \text{Class Period Rate: } 200\text{ gal/hr}; \quad \text{Horizontal: Zero usage}.
guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Confusing cumulative total volume with rate of consumption. A graph that is high on the vertical axis simply means a large total volume has been used since 6:00 AM. The rate of usage is determined solely by the slope (steepness) of the line.

guidedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Estimating Peak Flow from Derivative Rates
guidedExercises.problem: During a 30-minute lunch period from 11:30 AM to 12:00 PM ($0.5\text{ hours}$), water consumption surges by $1,200\text{ gallons}$. Compute the water consumption rate in gallons per minute (gpm).
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Convert the 30-minute interval into minutes to compute gallons per minute directly: $\text{Rate} = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t \text{ in min}}$.

steps.label: Compute gallons per minute
steps.explanation: During peak lunch rush, the building consumes 40 gallons of water every minute.

guidedExercises.finalAnswer: 40\text{ gallons per minute (gpm)} = 2,400\text{ gallons per hour}.
guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Mismatched units. When calculating rates, always specify the time unit (gallons per hour vs. gallons per minute). 40 gpm is equivalent to 2,400 gph.

exitTicket.title: Lesson 4 Exit Ticket: Analyzing Graphs—Water Usage During a Typical Day
exitTicket.prompt: Suppose the researchers collecting data for water consumption during a typical school day collected data through the night too. For the period between the time the last person leaves the building for the evening and the time of the arrival of the first person the next morning, how should the graph of water consumption appear? If the researchers also tracked rate of water consumption in gallons per hour, how would that graph look during the unoccupied night hours?
exitTicket.solution: The graph of cumulative water consumption should appear as a flat horizontal line because no water is being consumed while the building is empty. The rate of water consumption graph should sit on the horizontal axis at 0 gallons per hour.

problemSet.title: Official Worksheet: Problem Set & Practice
problemSet.description: Examine daily cyclical graphs, rate-of-change transitions, and temperature fluctuations.

problems.prompt:
A temperature graph for La Honda, CA recorded hourly temperatures across August and September. The graph exhibits repeated peaks and valleys.

(a) Explain why the graph alternates regularly between peaks and valleys.
(b) At approximately what time of day do the peaks typically occur? What about the valleys?
problems.solution:
(a) The graph alternates between peaks and valleys due to the Earth's diurnal day-night cycle: solar radiation warms the air during daytime hours, and heat radiates back into space at night.
(b) Peaks typically occur in the mid-to-late afternoon (around 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM) when thermal energy accumulation peaks, and valleys occur just before sunrise (around 5:00 AM - 6:00 AM) after continuous nocturnal cooling.

problems.prompt: If a graph shows the rate of water consumption in gallons per hour, how do you find the total water consumed over an interval where the rate is constant at 150 gal/hr for 4 hours?
problems.solution: \text{Total Volume} = \text{Rate} \times \text{Time} = 150\text{ gal/hr} \times 4\text{ hrs} = 600\text{ gallons}. On a rate-versus-time graph, this total corresponds to the rectangular area under the curve: 150 \times 4 = 600.
